♻ ☆ Simulation-free Unbalanced Dynamic Optimal Transport with General Growth Penalty
Junda Ying, Yuxuan Wang, Bowen Yang, Peijie Zhou, Lei Zhang
Inferring cellular dynamics from unpaired single-cell snapshots requires modeling both state transitions and population growth or death. Unbalanced dynamic optimal transport (UDOT) addresses this by penalizing growth along transport paths, making the choice of growth penalty a key way to encode biological priors on proliferation and apoptosis. However, existing UDOT solvers either rely on computationally expensive NeuralODE simulations or depend on analytical solutions of conditional paths, restricting their efficiency solely to quadratic penalties, i.e. Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geodesics. To enable an efficient UDOT solver for general growth penalties, we first show that concave growth penalties lead to degenerate solutions where growth and transport are separated. We then introduce \textbf{S}imulation-free \textbf{U}nbalanced \textbf{D}ynamic \textbf{O}ptimal transport (SUDO), a simulation-free framework for UDOT with general non-quadratic convex growth penalties. SUDO learns the conditional paths and transport costs, solves the induced semi-coupling problem, and subsequently leverages unbalanced flow matching to achieve a simulation-free solution. On WFR benchmarks, SUDO matches the accuracy of efficient, analytical solution-driven algorithms while outperforming simulation-based methods in computational speed. Beyond WFR, SUDO supports asymmetric penalties that encode proliferation-dominant priors and produce more plausible trajectories and growth estimates on synthetic and single-cell datasets.
♻ ☆ Neuromorphic Navigation in Static and Dynamic Environments with Dual-Timescale Neuron-Astrocyte Memory
Yuliya Tsybina, Evgenia Antonova, Sergey Shchanikov, Vsevolod Kulagin, Alexey Mikhaylov, Victor Kazantsev, Vyacheslav Demin, Susanna Gordleeva
Biological agents navigate complex environments by combining long-term memory of successful actions with short-term suppression of recently visited locations-a capability difficult to replicate in artificial systems. We introduce a neuromorphic navigation system based on a spiking neuron--astrocyte network (SNAN), in which spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) reinforces traversed action sequences on a long timescale, while astrocytic calcium transients suppress moves into recently visited states on a short timescale. This dual-timescale memory biases the agent toward unexplored regions without reward signals or explicit global statistics. In grid worlds where the agent observes only its current position, astrocytic modulation increased goal completion from 45.9% to 99.9% and shortened median routes 5.8-15-fold on commonly solved tasks. Compared with seven classical strategies, including Tremaux's and Tarry's algorithms and tabular Q-learning, SNAN yields the shortest routes among reliable strategies in open and sparse static mazes while storing 2.8-4.6 times fewer variables than memory-based baselines. In dynamic mazes, its decaying memory retains no obsolete passage marks, so SNAN becomes more efficient as the topology changes. After ten learning cycles, STDP makes SNAN the best reliable strategy. The astrocytic modulation mitigates the exploration-exploitation trade-off through local state suppression, a form of working memory we term Topological-Context Memory. To validate hardware feasibility, we map STDP to a memristive VTEAM model and implement a subset of the network on a crossbar array, achieving order-of-magnitude gains in speed per area and energy per decision over CPU implementations. These results establish astrocyte-inspired dual-timescale memory as a compact, hardware-compatible principle for neuromorphic navigation.
♻ ☆ The Mean First-Reaction Time on a Thin Filament in a 3-D Domain
Denis S. Grebenkov, Theodore Kolokolnikov, Alan E. Lindsay, Michael J. Ward
We study the mean first-reaction time (MFRT) of a Brownian particle in a bounded three-dimensional domain $Ω$ with a reflecting boundary $\partialΩ$, that contains a thin reactive filament. The filament is a tube of cross-sectional diameter $\varepsilon\ll 1$ around a smooth closed curve $Γ$, and its surface is partially reactive with reactivity $b$. As $\varepsilon\to 0$ the filament reduces to a line source in the outer problem. Its cross-section enters only through a logarithmic reactive capacitance $d_c(b)$, so that the MFRT is O$(-\log[\varepsilon d_c])$. This contrasts with the $O(\varepsilon^{-1})$ scaling for spatially localized traps of radius $\varepsilon$. Using matched asymptotic expansions, we derive a Fredholm integral equation on $Γ$ for the line density of the reactive flux. It sums all powers of $ν\equiv -1/\log[\varepsilon d_c]$ and involves two geometric quantities: the regular part $R$ of the Neumann Green's function, which encodes the interaction of $Γ$ with $\partialΩ$, and an intrinsic self-energy of $Γ$ that depends only on its shape. The framework extends to multiple filaments, splitting probabilities, a spatially heterogeneous diffusivity, and the principal eigenvalue of the Laplacian. For the unit sphere we solve the integral equation with a simple trapezoidal Nyström scheme, and we validate the predictions for rings, linked rings and torus knots against full 3-D finite-element solutions.
♻ ☆ Structural identifiability of partially-observed stochastic processes: from single-particle trajectories to total particle density data
Arianna Ceccarelli, Alexander P. Browning, Ruth E. Baker
The increasing availability of experimental data has intensified interest in calibrating stochastic models, raising fundamental questions about parameter identifiability. Structural identifiability determines whether parameters can be uniquely recovered from idealised data, a prerequisite to allow for parameter estimation in real-world scenarios. However, there is a lack of methodologies generally applicable to analyse the structural identifiability of such stochastic processes. Therefore, we develop a methodology for a class of spatio-temporal stochastic processes. We investigate how structural identifiability depends on the type of available data, distinguishing between single-particle trajectories and total particle density measurements. For trajectory data, we use a particle-based description that explicitly represents single-particle dynamics. For population-level data, we derive a partial differential equation representation, that describes the evolution of total particle density, and apply a differential algebra approach, common to ordinary differential equation analysis. We further introduce Taylor-series-expansion and Fourier-transform approaches to study the initial condition. We apply our methodology to an example model with a specified class of initial conditions. We show that the model is globally structurally identifiable given infinitely many, infinitely long single-particle trajectories, but only locally structurally identifiable from total particle density data, demonstrating that parameter identifiability depends on the type of data available.

♻ ☆ Open Biomedical Knowledge Graphs at Scale: Construction, Federation, and AI Agent Access with Samyama Graph Database
Madhulatha Mandarapu, Sandeep Kunkunuru
Biomedical knowledge is fragmented across siloed databases---Reactome, STRING, Gene Ontology, ClinicalTrials.gov, DrugBank, DGIdb, SIDER, PubMed, ClinVar, ChEMBL, OpenTargets, and more. We present an open, reproducible biomedical knowledge graph ecosystem built on Samyama, a Rust-native graph database: three foundational graphs detailed end-to-end---Pathways KG (118,686 nodes, 834,785 edges), Clinical Trials KG (7,774,446 nodes, 26,973,997 edges), and Drug Interactions KG (32,726 nodes, 191,970 edges)---and their expansion into a 22-graph, 2-cohort merged biomedical store (328,130,739 nodes and 1,441,425,733 imported edges, including 295,000 synthetic OMOP CDM patients from Synthea). First, we describe a reproducible ETL and portable .sgsnap snapshot pattern where graphs load alone or compose into one store. Second, we analyze single-store cross-KG integration via query-time property joins and load-time identifier deduplication (--dedup-keys): across all 24 snapshots (Samyama-Graph v1.13.0), 328.1M nodes and 1.44B edges load in 2,269.1 s (37m 49s) within 366.5 GB peak RSS (254 B/edge), merging 132,511 cross-source entities across five audited keys (mondo_id,uniprot_id,go_id,drugbank_id,symbol)---87.8% of the 150,965 Bound A sound-identifier ceiling, with zero conflicting-ID refusals. On a frozen 81-query suite, 62 queries return results (17 data-gap empties, 2 timeouts); on an expanded 200-query oracle suite, 195 of 200 pass (97.5%). Third, we introduce schema-driven Model Context Protocol (MCP) server generation: on the 40-question BiomedQA benchmark over the 3-KG subset, domain-specific MCP tools achieve 98% accuracy vs. 85% for schema-aware text-to-Cypher and 75% for standalone GPT-4o, with zero schema errors.

☆ AI-driven structural informatics reveals diverse glycosylation machinery across double-stranded DNA viruses
Lan Na
Glycosylation is widespread in biology and shapes molecular recognition, yet the diversity and biosynthetic organization of viral glycosyltransferases (GTs) remain poorly understood. Here we integrate structural-alphabet-guided searches and structure similarity networks with genomic-neighbourhood and biosynthetic gene cluster embedding analyses to examine viral GT-A proteins. This approach reveals extensive structural diversity overlooked by sequence-based annotation, including previously uncharacterized viral GT lineages. Most strikingly, we identified a jumbo-phage locus encoding five tandem glycosyltransferases alongside hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine biosynthetic and sulfation-associated enzymes, suggesting a previously unrecognized form of viral DNA modification involving a sulfated pentasaccharide. Beyond these examples, predicted saccharide-associated loci span divergent double-stranded DNA viruses, from giant viruses to tailed phages, and occupy multiple regions of the reference biosynthetic landscape. Together, our findings uncover an underappreciated repertoire of virus-encoded glycosylation machinery and suggest that viral glycan biosynthesis encompasses diverse molecular contexts and potential biological functions.
☆ D2ML: Models for Direct-to-Biology Small Molecule Screening NeurIPS 2026
AkshatKumar Nigam, Neri Amara, Hillary Dequina, Dyana Kenanova, Seth Malmersjo, Fiorella Ruggiu, Raymond V. Fucini, Jack Sadowsky, Stig K. Hansen, Imran S. Haque
Direct-to-biology (D2B) screening enables rapid testing of newly synthesized molecules without purification. However, uncertain concentrations in crude mixtures and limited purified-compound measurements complicate the use of these data in machine learning. Here we show that models tailored to the structure of D2B data can improve prediction and guide the discovery of more potent and selective compounds. Our assay-aware models predict activity from single-point screens, relative potency across targets from crude dose-response assays, and absolute potency from purified-compound measurements. For crude assays, potency ratios between targets tested from the same well can retain selectivity information despite uncertain concentrations. A joint model that shares information across stages and balances their contributions to training improved predictions over separate neural networks. The largest gain was in crude dose-response selectivity prediction, where rank correlation increased from 0.27 to 0.40. In a separate experiment, independently trained models guided the selection of 84 new compounds to improve ROS1 potency while limiting activity against the anti-target TRKB. Synthesis and testing identified compounds that extended the measured Pareto front, achieving better combinations of potency and selectivity than those in the training data. The most selective new compound achieved a ROS1 IC50 of 14.7 nM and 233-fold selectivity over TRKB. By comparison, the most selective training compound had a ROS1 IC50 of 20.3 nM and 79-fold selectivity. ATLAS provides the experimental setting for this approach, supporting synthesis and screening of 1,000-10,000 model-selected compounds in two- to three-week cycles. Together, these results show how assay-aware learning can use the full D2B assay sequence to guide multi-objective molecular optimization.

♻ ☆ Core physical principles of allostery
Eric Rouviere, Olivier Rivoire, Rama Ranganathan
Allostery is a basic property of proteins that represents the functional coupling of distantly positioned amino acids. In different manifestations, this property underlies signal transmission, cooperative binding, regulation, catalysis, and evolvability---the elementary features of molecular processes in living cells. While thermodynamic models have provided excellent abstract phenomenological descriptions and classifications of allostery, comparable descriptions and classifications at a more microscopic level, where the nature of physical interactions is specified, are lacking. Starting from minimal assumptions, we derive the essential physical principles of allostery and show that previously described forms of allostery can be viewed as specific implementations of a combination of two core principles: actuation of a soft mode and switching between two states. Organizing allostery by these principles may provide a simpler and more universal language to describe the physics of allostery in proteins.
♻ ☆ CMADiff: Cross-Modal Aligned Diffusion for Controllable Protein Generation
Changjian Zhou, Xinyue Zhang, Yuexi Qiu, Jiaqing Zhang, Heng-Da Cheng, Jia Song, Wensheng Xiang

However, most existing models primarily utilize protein sequence or structural data for training, neglecting the physicochemical properties of proteins.Moreover, they are deficient to control the generation of proteins in intuitive conditions. To address these limitations,we propose CMADiff here, a novel framework that enables controllable protein generation by aligning the physicochemical properties of protein sequences with text-based descriptions through a latent diffusion process. In this latent space, we apply a conditional diffusion process, which is guided by BioAligner, a contrastive learning-based module that aligns text descriptions with protein features, enabling text-driven control over protein sequence generation. The implementation and code are available at https://github.com/HPC-NEAU/PhysChemDiff.

♻ ☆ When Does Context Help? A Systematic Study of Target-Conditional Molecular Property Prediction
Bryan Cheng, Jasper Zhang
We present the first systematic study of when target context helps molecular property prediction, evaluating context conditioning across 10 diverse protein families, 4 fusion architectures, data regimes spanning 67-9,409 training compounds, and both temporal and random evaluation splits. Using NestDrug, a FiLM-based architecture that conditions molecular representations on target identity, we characterize both success and failure modes with three principal findings. First, fusion architecture dominates: FiLM outperforms concatenation by 24.2 percentage points and additive conditioning by 8.6 pp; how you incorporate context matters more than whether you include it. Second, context enables otherwise impossible predictions: on data-scarce CYP3A4 (67 training compounds), multi-task transfer achieves 0.686 AUC where per-target Random Forest collapses to 0.238. Third, context can systematically hurt: distribution mismatch causes 10.2 pp degradation on BACE1; few-shot adaptation consistently underperforms zero-shot. Beyond methodology, we expose fundamental flaws in standard benchmarking: 1-nearest-neighbor Tanimoto achieves 0.991 AUC on DUD-E without any learning, and 50% of actives leak from training data, rendering absolute performance metrics meaningless. Our temporal split evaluation (train up to 2020, test 2021-2024) achieves stable 0.843 AUC with no degradation, providing the first rigorous evidence that context-conditional molecular representations generalize to future chemical space.

♻ ☆ Predicting Dose-Response Success from Primary Screening Data
Sean Lim
High-throughput drug screening uses inexpensive primary screens to select compounds for more costly follow-up dose-response experiments, which estimate compound potency (pXC50) by determining the concentration required to produce a specified biological effect. However, many promoted compounds fail to yield a reportable potency, even when activity is subsequently confirmed. We investigated whether inexpensive three-point primary-screening data could predict whether a more costly 11-point dose-response experiment would yield a reportable pXC50. Using a dataset of 32,971 compound-assay pairs with three-point primary-screening and 11-point dose-response measurements, we trained random-forest models to predict successful potency quantification. Our model achieved an AUROC of 0.939 +/- 0.002 and generalized to previously unseen chemical scaffolds and assay-mechanism families. We found that primary-screen response features were more predictive of dose-response quantifiability than molecular structure-based features. Successful potency quantification was also strongly associated with primary-screen response amplitude. Across eight chronological test releases, the model retrospectively retained 90% of reportable potencies while selecting only 55.7% of historically promoted compound-assay pairs for follow-up profiling. These findings suggest that predicting potency quantifiability from primary-screening data could improve the efficiency of compound prioritization and reduce unnecessary dose-response experiments.

☆ A heterogenetic theory of living systems
Alessandro Sarti, Giovanna Citti
The problem of the dynamics of living systems and their mathematical representation essentially unfolds on two levels. Firstly, the principles of autopoiesis and operational closure describe how a living system produces and maintains itself. Secondly, living phenomena are recognised as historical, involving the evolution of dynamics and spaces of possibility that change over time. Currently, no differential model can incorporate both of these aspects. We propose adopting the differential heterogenesis framework, which enables us to define differential operators that change in space and time, producing event-based and historical dynamics. In this construction, heterogeneous operator assemblages will be constrained by the principles of autopoiesis and operational closure, providing a theoretical framework for event-based and historical living systems. Finally, we provide a specific example of assembly with Gray-Scott kinetic equations, along with numerical simulations and results.

☆ Yoga biomechanics through energy optimization: diverse kinematics and low-dimensional kinetics
Sriram Sekaripuram Muralidhar, Manoj Srinivasan
Yoga is widely practiced for improving physical and mental health, yet the biomechanical demands of individual yoga poses remain poorly characterized. Existing experimental studies typically examine only a small number of poses or muscles, limiting their ability to guide pose selection for rehabilitation or exercise prescription. Here we present a computational framework for predicting whole-body joint torques and contact forces from two-dimensional images of yoga poses. The framework combines manual pose digitization, a sagittal-plane MuJoCo human model, and constrained metabolic energy minimization subject to static equilibrium. We applied the framework to 55 sagittally symmetric yoga poses from Light on Yoga, generating a dataset of joint kinematics, contact locations, and predicted joint torques and contact forces. These poses collectively span nearly the full physiological range of motion of the major joints while exhibiting a wide range of predicted joint torques, with the greatest average demands on the lower extremities and lumbar region. Thus, yoga poses exhibit substantial diversity in body configurations but comparatively low-dimensional patterns of predicted joint loading. Predicted joint torque rankings were also largely insensitive to uncertainty in the relative weighting of joint metabolic costs. This framework enables systematic biomechanical analysis of yoga poses and provides a foundation for quantitatively evaluating their mechanical demands and informing future rehabilitation strategies.

☆ PCR-ALERA: A PCR-ELISA analogue but antibody-free DNA detection system
Miles Bonenberger, Roland Krämer
PCR-ALERA is a new concept for DNA detection that combines DNA amplification by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with an activator-linked enzyme reactivation assay (ALERA). PCR-ALERA resembles the commercial, semi-quantitative PCR-ELISA assay that offers high sensitivity and high-throughput screening in microplates. PCR-ALERA overcomes a major drawback of PCR-ELISA since it does not require the time-consuming handling of expensive antibodies. In the first step of the assay, commercially available modified nucleotides were incorporated during PCR amplification of the target DNA. A selenocysteine containing peptide (the activator) was linked to the amplified DNA by click chemistry. This peptide has been optimized for the highly efficient activation of the latent protease papain by selenolate-triggered disulfide cleavage. The DNA-peptide hybrid was then immoblized in microplate wells and incubated with latent papain. The latter was readily activated and converted a fluorogenic substrate to a fluorescent product with high catalytic turnover. Overall assay time is about 4 hours including PCR.

☆ Beyond $χ^2$: Ensemble null tests for reliable scientific discovery
Adrian E. Bayer, David N. Spergel
Unrecognized systematic errors can survive standard checks and undermine scientific discoveries. Null tests and experimental controls can expose these failures, but averaging measurements or reducing them to scalar statistics can hide important structure. We propose ensemble null tests that compare multivariate distributions with references from observations or simulations. We demonstrate their benefits across science. In cosmic microwave background simulations, they detect systematic effects missed by conventional $χ^2$ tests. In Gaia data, they detect velocity asymmetry as sensitively as an informed search. In a CRISPR screen, they expose a control mismatch in DNA damage and reveal which cellular profiles drive it. As scientific datasets grow, ensemble testing turns repeated measurements into a broader search for unknown unknowns, strengthening the empirical foundation for scientific discovery.

We argue that verification, not generation, is the binding constraint, and that better models will not relieve it. Confirming a structure to the field's own standard means having the molecule in hand. Automation can lower what that costs per compound, but the cost stays proportional to the number of structures and never amortizes across them. Two substitutes are on offer and neither removes that requirement. In-silico spectral prediction ranks candidates instead of confirming one, and the strongest current model puts the right structure first 33.5% of the time on a scaffold-split benchmark. Any assignment resting on spectral similarity is, by the field's own definition, made without a reference standard. Microcrystal diffraction does return a structure, but it needs the compound to crystallize out of a trace mixture, which is a different problem rather than an easier one. We sorted 10,645 computationally inferred metabolite structures by what verifying each would take. Between 5% and 37% have no verification route identified under our analysis. That spread reflects where the thresholds are set rather than a measured count of unverifiable compounds, and the inaccessible ones cluster among the most speculative entries. Those figures understate the problem, because the gut makes far more compounds than any database records. HMDB holds only what someone has already thought worth cataloguing, and structure generators are bounded by nothing at all. The claim is easy to disprove. Show a route that confirms structures as fast as they are proposed. Until someone does, two problems stay unsolved. Nobody knows how to spend a verification budget that will always be too small, or what a biologist may conclude from a structure that was never confirmed.

Because this shift mixes measurement error with selection shift, we decompose and simulate both on the cohort's window structure. Filtering lowers local error when error depends on confidence, but biases the endpoint once confidence tracks movement more than error. In the Parkinson-related data, confidence was only weakly tied to movement (rho = 0.14). There, filtering is harmless if well-tracked windows are unbiased. If instead systematic error only redistributes within participants, filtering can add up to 0.58 degrees. Here, we test these assumptions in seven public datasets of human gait (71 participants), including 16 people who both walked and ran. We fit linear step-to-step maps and validate them by cross-validation, holding out more data where more data exist. At first sight, gait has memory: the state two steps back lowers the prediction error by up to 29\%. Yet most of this temporal coupling vanishes once the operating point may drift slowly and measurement noise is modelled; gait remains limit-cycle-like, around an operating point that moves. Running keeps more memory than walking in the same people. Spatial coupling between the planes is present in most participants, mainly from sagittal to frontal, but weak. This supports planar models of healthy gait, while a repeatable, task-dependent coupling index may serve as a measure of gait quality. The simple models are wrong, but useful enough.

☆ What to randomize matters: a controlled study of volume, axis and representation in low-data molecular generation
Neerav Kaushal, Alisa Teige, Ajay MNV Penmatsa
Chemical language models can struggle to generate new molecules when trained on small datasets, where a model may reproduce training examples rather than learn a useful generative distribution. Randomized SMILES augmentation varies atom traversal, whereas Sequential Attachment-based Fragment Embedding (SAFE) also allows the order of fragment blocks to vary. How these distinct sources of representational variation affect low-data molecular generation has not been clearly studied. Here, using 1,000 seed molecules to train an autoregressive sequence model, we compare canonical SAFE with randomized SAFE at increasing corpus sizes, isolate atom-order and fragment-order axes of SAFE randomization, and compare fully randomized SAFE with randomized SMILES at molecule-by-molecule matched training corpora. Three findings emerge. First, randomization of SAFE alone raises the genuine yield of novel molecules more than 450-fold, turning a model that merely reproduces its training set into a practical molecular generator. Second, the two axes of randomization act jointly rather than additively: atom order alone reaches a tenth, and fragment order alone a seventh, of the genuine yield obtained when both vary, which is four times their combined contribution. Third, at matched corpus size and compute, randomized SAFE delivers 2.8 times the genuine yield of randomized SMILES. Welch tests with Games-Howell post-hoc comparisons resolve every difference on the primary outcomes. In the low-data regime, thus, what one randomizes rather than only how much determines whether augmentation produces new molecules or merely new spellings of the training set.

☆ The Mean First-Reaction Time on a Thin Filament in a 3-D Domain
Denis S. Grebenkov, Theodore Kolokolnikov, Alan E. Lindsay, Michael J. Ward
We study the mean first-reaction time (MFRT) of a Brownian particle in a bounded three-dimensional domain $Ω$ with a reflecting boundary $\partialΩ$, that contains a thin reactive filament. The filament is a tube of cross-sectional diameter $\varepsilon\ll 1$ around a smooth closed curve $Γ$, and its surface is partially reactive with reactivity $b$. As $\varepsilon\to 0$ the filament reduces to a line source in the outer problem. Its cross-section enters only through a logarithmic reactive capacitance $d_c(b)$, so that the MFRT is $\mathcal{O}(-\log[\varepsilon d_c])$. This contrasts with the $\mathcal{O}(\eps^{-1})$ scaling for spatially localized traps of radius $\eps$. Using matched asymptotic expansions, we derive a Fredholm integral equation on $Γ$ for the line density of the reactive flux. It sums all powers of $ν\equiv -1/\log[\varepsilon d_c]$ and involves two geometric quantities: the regular part $R$ of the Neumann Green's function, which encodes the interaction of $Γ$ with $\partialΩ$, and an intrinsic self-energy of $Γ$ that depends only on its shape. The framework extends to multiple filaments, splitting probabilities, a spatially heterogeneous diffusivity, and the principal eigenvalue of the Laplacian. For the unit sphere we solve the integral equation with a simple trapezoidal Nyström scheme, and we validate the predictions for rings, linked rings and torus knots against full 3-D finite-element solutions.

The framework utilizes the submartingale structure of the loss function's Hessian and tracks its minimum eigenvalue over time. Under convergence of the time-averaged Hessian, we prove that this eigenvalue grows linearly for identifiable models, but only sublinearly, as $o(t)$, for unidentifiable ones; for a specific type of parameter redundancy, this $o(t)$ bound is tightened to $o(\sqrt{t}\log t)$. Applying the framework to stochastic flocking models, we demonstrate that, in identifiable settings, the magnitude of the eigenvalue reflects the attainable estimation precision. We further uncover a physical mechanism of unidentifiability: as the system approaches the ordered state, the parameters become algebraically degenerate, even though the model contains no trivial redundancy. Identifiability therefore depends on the dynamical regime, not only on model structure. Our framework offers a practical tool for reliable parameter estimation, not only in flocking models but in SDE models across diverse fields.

For $Λ$ < 1 the first receptor to activate does so before its ligand has ever dissociated, and the Weibull law holds. As $Λ$ grows, activation relies increasingly on repeated unbinding and rebinding. The true activation time then exceeds the Weibull prediction by up to 2900-fold on our parameter grid, and the effective Weibull shape falls to one, so activation becomes memoryless instead of timer-like. We derive a closed form that keeps koff by treating the successful pass through the proofreading chain separately from the time lost to failed attempts. It matches exact medians to within 2% in 19 of 25 parameter sets, with a worst case of about 6%, and reproduces the loss of timer-like behavior. Because $Λ$ is computed from the Weibull prediction itself, it shows in advance how far that formula can be trusted; where it cannot, the new expression requires only a one-dimensional root find.

♻ ☆ From static structures to dynamic landscapes: cryo-EM redefines RNA biology
Shekhar Jadhav, Spandan Saha, Qingbin Shang, Marco Marcia
RNA molecules perform diverse biological functions by dynamically exploring multiple conformational states rather than adopting a single static structure. Capturing these ensembles is a challenge in molecular biology. Recent advances in cryoEM are now transforming this landscape by enabling the visualization of RNA molecules across a broad spectrum of functionally relevant conformations at near atomic resolution. Here, we examine how cryoEM is reshaping RNA structural biology changing focus from the analysis of static structures to dynamic conformational landscapes. Through 8 representative case studies we illustrate how cryoEM has revealed previously inaccessible mechanisms of RNA motion, including folding processes, ligand-dependent switching, and cooperative assembly. We specifically discuss emerging experimental and computational approaches that address and overcome the challenges associated with studying dynamic RNAs, particularly in construct design, sample preparation, vitrification, and data analysis. These novel methods resolve conformational variability and enable the reconstruction of discrete and continuous RNA conformational landscapes from cryoEM data, highlighting how structural heterogeneity can be harnessed to extract functional insights. Looking forward, the integration of cryoEM with complementary biophysical techniques and time resolved methodologies promises to bridge structural and temporal resolution, to routinely derive experimental molecular movies of RNA in action. These advances will not only deepen our understanding of RNA biology but also provide new opportunities for RNA targeted therapeutics and the rational design of dynamic RNA-based nanodevices. By connecting structural snapshots into coherent dynamic models, cryoEM is establishing a framework for quantitative descriptions of RNA energy landscapes and their functional roles.
♻ ☆ Commutative Algebra Modeling of Mutation and Disease Association
JunJie Wee, Mushal Zia, Faisal Suwayyid, Hongsong Feng, Yuta Hozumi, Guo-Wei Wei
Genetic mutations can lead to disease by disrupting molecular interactions, altering protein stability, inducing misfolding, and promoting protein aggregation. Although existing predictive models have achieved promising performance, they often lack mechanistic interpretability and fail to fully incorporate the underlying physical and chemical principles governing mutation-induced effects. Moreover, current approaches typically address disease association, protein stability changes, and solubility alterations as separate prediction tasks rather than integrating them within a unified framework. In this study, we introduce a multiscale commutative algebra modeling framework for predicting disease-mutation association. Leveraging persistent Stanley-Reisner theory, we extract algebraic invariants to build two predictive models: Commutative Algebra Neural Network (CANet) and Commutative Algebra Gradient Boosting Tree (CATree). The proposed framework is applied to three biologically connected tasks: disease-associated mutation identification, mutation-induced protein stability change prediction, and mutation-induced protein solubility change classification. Across six benchmark tasks, CANet and CATree consistently achieve leading predictive performance, with up to 7.5% relative improvement over existing methods. These results demonstrate that commutative algebra provides a unified, interpretable, and generalizable modeling strategy for mutation-disease association prediction.

☆ HGPRGDel: GPR-Aware Learning and Ranking for Growth-Coupled Gene Deletion Design

Designing microbial strains for growth-coupled production, in which cellular growth is linked to the synthesis of a target compound through genetic interventions, is a fundamental goal in metabolic engineering. Constraint-based methods can identify growth-coupled deletion strategies, but design for each target typically requires a separate search across a large number of possible gene-deletion combinations. This motivates a reusable approach that learns from previously evaluated strain designs to prioritize candidate interventions before downstream constraint-based evaluation. We present a reproducible protocol for growth-coupled gene deletion design that learns and ranks gene-deletion priorities for each target metabolite. Using computationally curated deletion strategies as learning resources, the protocol generates continuous deletion-priority rankings, constructs candidate strategies at adjustable search-space budgets, and evaluates these candidates through constraint-based metabolic analysis. Its learning component, HGPRGDel, explicitly represents gene-protein-reaction (GPR) logic, capturing how multiple genes can jointly support a reaction or alternative genes can maintain its activity, while integrating molecular and reaction-level information. Across e_coli_core, iMM904, and iML1515, the protocol achieves the highest macro-F1 and AUC among the evaluated learning configurations. HGPRGDel's rankings recovered an average of 90% of the reference deletion genes from MetNetComp by examining fewer genes than the evaluated baseline methods. By separating learned intervention prioritization from downstream constraint-based assessment, the protocol provides a reproducible framework for reusing strain-design knowledge while controlling the size of the candidate space and retaining mechanistic evaluation of growth-coupled production.
☆ pyTransRate: 1 reference-free quality assessment of de novo transcriptome assemblies with current aligners and quantifiers
Matthew MacManes
Summary: The original software TransRate scores a de novo transcriptome assembly by mapping the reads it was built from back to it, with no reference required. Its last release (1.0.3) depends on Ruby 2.2 and on aligner and quantifier versions that can no longer be installed on most systems. pyTransRate is a Python reimplementation of the TransRate method built on snap-aligner 2.0.5 and salmon 2.7.0. In 5,031 paired comparisons (39 assembly-level metrics on each of 129 public assemblies), it reproduces the original sequence metrics and read counts exactly and ranks assemblies consistently with 1.0.3 (Spearman rho = 0.94 for assembly score, 0.98 for good-mapping rate), although its read-based scores are not numerically interchangeable with the original. It also reads gzip- and bgzip-compressed input directly. Availability and Implementation: pyTransRate is implemented in Python 3 and is freely available under the MIT license at https://github.com/macmanes-lab/pytransrate. It runs on Linux and macOS; snap-aligner and salmon are installed from Bioconda. Supplementary information: Supplementary data are available online. Supplementary Table S1 lists the assembly and read accessions for every assembly analyzed; Supplementary Table S2 gives per-assembly values from both implementations.
☆ Stationary Action Principles for Neuronal Growth
Nathan Brodeur, Cristian Staii
Neuronal growth is guided by biochemical, mechanical, and geometrical cues while being influenced by stochastic fluctuations in cytoskeletal dynamics, adhesion, and growth cone sensing. Here, we develop two complementary variational descriptions of mechanically guided axonal growth. First, for neurons growing on periodic parallel micropatterns, we use Langevin and Fokker--Planck models to derive a stochastic path action incorporating deterministic substrate guidance and random fluctuations. The probability of a growth trajectory decreases exponentially with this action, and the most probable trajectories correspond to minimum action paths for fixed boundary conditions. Second, for axons growing on substrates with spatially varying stiffness, we show that stiffness dependent traction generates mechanical guidance and axonal turning at stiffness interfaces. In the quasi-static limit, this response leads to a Fermat-like spatial action with an effective axonal refractive index determined by the traction and substrate stiffness relationship. The resulting framework predicts axonal refraction across stiffness boundaries, including an approximate Snell-like relation and a critical angle condition. Although the stochastic and Fermat-like actions have distinct physical meanings and ranges of validity, both describe how substrate mechanics constrain axonal trajectories. These results connect measurable quantities, including drift, diffusion, stiffness, traction, and growth direction, to global properties of axonal paths and provide a framework for designing biomimetic substrates for controlled neuronal growth and regeneration.

The solver combines finite-strain extensible-director shells, hyperelastic constitutive models, and a finite-range repulsive contact energy. Nonlinear equilibrium is solved using a regularized, matrix-free Newton-Krylov method with two-level preconditioning. Automatic differentiation evaluates tangent-vector products without forming or storing the primary tangent matrix, while GPU execution parallelizes element and quadrature-point computations. Constitutive, shell, contact, and self-contact responses were assessed against analytical, semi-analytical, and published benchmarks. At a contact-free plate equilibrium, implicit sensitivities of the converged apex displacement to constitutive parameters, thickness, and pressure agreed with finite differences from independent nonlinear simulations. Simulations of three patient-specific aortic-valve models (two tricuspid and one bicuspid) achieved final relative equilibrium residuals below 10^-4. Median GPU runtimes were approximately 15-25 minutes, with 5.3-6.5-fold speedups relative to corresponding CPU runs on the tested hardware. These results provide component-level verification and demonstrate GPU-accelerated forward valve simulation in the tested cases, supporting future gradient-based inverse studies.
♻ ☆ A general-purpose multi-path stacked coupling for stochastic reaction networks
David F. Anderson, Jingyi Ma
Stochastic reaction networks are continuous-time Markov chain models for interacting populations, with applications in biochemistry, epidemiology, ecology, and related areas. Coupling multiple stochastic reaction networks effectively is a fundamental challenge in stochastic simulation. Existing variance-reducing coupling methods are typically designed for pairs of processes, though specialized multi-path constructions have been developed for particular applications. To fill this gap, we introduce the multi-path stacked coupling (MSC), a space-time Poisson construction that jointly simulates a finite collection of stochastic reaction networks with common reaction channels and reaction vectors, but possibly different intensity functions and initial conditions. Each pairwise marginal of MSC has the same law as the corresponding split-coupled pair, allowing existing variance bounds to transfer directly; in finite-state settings, we also obtain first-order expansions for the mean and second moment of finite-difference numerators. We demonstrate the framework through three sensitivity estimation tasks requiring several nearby parameterized paths: estimating many first derivatives simultaneously, estimating a single first derivative using a wider finite-difference stencil, and estimating higher-order derivatives. Numerical experiments on a processive phosphorylation network demonstrate strong performance in each of the three application areas considered, consistent with the theoretical advantages of MSC: across all three applications, MSC achieves the smallest root mean square error (RMSE) among the methods considered over the tested computational budgets.

♻ ☆ Dynamic heart rate variability for classification of arrhythmia burden

Purpose: Heart rate variability (HRV) may provide information beyond heart rate (HR) for identifying arrhythmia burden, but the value of temporal HRV variation remains unclear. This study developed a dynamic HRV measure quantifying the interquartile range of window-level root mean square of successive RR-interval differences (IQRRMSSD) and evaluated its utility in classifying total abnormal-beat and premature ventricular contraction (PVC) burden compared with the conventional RR-based HRV measure, RMSSD. Methods: Manually annotated 30-minute ECG recordings from 43 individuals were analyzed using overlapping windows. A linear support vector classifier was used to classify individuals as having high or low arrhythmia burden, defined using 1% and 10% burden thresholds. Four feature sets were evaluated: HR alone, HR with RMSSD, HR with IQRRMSSD, and all three measures. Performance was assessed using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation. At the 1% threshold, IQRRMSSD showed particularly high sensitivity for total abnormal-beat and PVC burden ($0.970 \pm 0.064$ and $0.882 \pm 0.193$, respectively). At the 10% threshold, conventional RMSSD showed the strongest overall discrimination, achieving a ROC-AUC of 0.947 for PVC burden. Combined features sometimes improved the sensitivity-specificity balance but not overall discrimination. Conclusion: These findings suggest that a conventional RR-based HRV measure is informative for elevated ectopic burden, while a dynamic HRV measure may provide complementary information for lower-burden abnormalities.

Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) has become a standard approach for label-free microscopy of transparent specimens, mapping the optical path length. However, the isotropic phase is blind to the molecular order underlying optical anisotropy. Implementations that also add quantitative contrast to birefringence rely on multi-frame illumination or polarization-state scanning, or on dedicated interferometric hardware and thus trade away acquisition speed or the simplicity of a standard microscope. We developed a new globally regularized phase reconstruction that eliminates artifacts of prior DIC-to-QPI approaches, providing quantitative phase information, and used per-pixel Stokes-based reconstruction to obtain quantitative anisotropic retardance. We validate the approach across simulations, static reference targets, fixed muscle tissue and living dynamically moving cells. QPPI enables all-optical and label-free studies of contractile dynamics in live cardiomyocytes. It provides both structural and functional readouts at sufficient frame rates to resolve fast cardiomyocyte contractions. Conventional fluorescent labels bleach over time, perturb physiology, and preclude long-term monitoring. Instead, QPPI enables long-term, label-free interrogation of dynamic cellular processes at quantitative contrast and provides structural readouts similar to those provided by established fluorescent labels, such as frame-by-frame sarcomere length. It also offers previously inaccessible measurements, like quantitative analysis of retardance changes during muscle contraction, which provides a direct optical signature of muscle photoelasticity.
♻ ☆ Multiscale MIGHT: Modeling Local and Systemic Particle Transport in the Cardiovascular System
Theofilos Symeonidis, Timo Jakumeit, Fardad Vakilipoor, Robert Schober, Maximilian Schäfer
Analytical models of signaling molecule (SM) transport in the cardiovascular system (CVS) force a choice between whole-body scope and vessel-level resolution: Pharmacokinetic models for systemic transport lump each organ and lack small-scale structure, whereas synthetic molecular communication (MC) channel models resolve branched vessel networks (VNs) only for a single pass or capture recirculation only in topologically simple loops, and only partially include SM degradation. To close this gap, we propose Multiscale MIGHT, an extension of the Mixture of Inverse Gaussians for Hemodynamic Transport (MIGHT) model that jointly captures branched topologies, closed-loop circulation, organ clearance, and chemical degradation of SMs. First, we connect the ends of a branched VN to form a closed loop with local and global SM degradation, model the closed-loop channel impulse response for arbitrary transmitter (Tx) and receiver (Rx) positions as a Laplace-domain feedback system, and approximate it in closed form by an inverse Gaussian mixture over multi-pass trajectories. The model is validated against finite-element simulations in COMSOL. Second, we set up a whole-body model, where an exemplary local VN, resolved at vessel-level detail, is embedded into the remaining systemic circulation, represented by lumped organ blocks. We simulate whole-body SM transport for various Tx sites and SM species. Our results show that, at an Rx in a local VN, only the initial pass produces a distinct peak in the SM concentration, significantly shaped by the local vasculature in case of small Tx-Rx distances; subsequent passes arrive strongly dispersed and are shaped almost entirely by organ clearance and chemical degradation rather than by the local VN topology.

♻ ☆ Reading Between the Reads: A Decade On, Revisiting Sequencing Protocol Annotation in the Sequence Read Archive
Jamie J. Alnasir
Background: Experimental metadata are essential for interpreting archived sequencing data. In 2015, Alnasir and Shanahan examined the annotation of fragmentation, adapter ligation and enrichment in the Sequence Read Archive (SRA). This study revisits those measurements using the original SQL keyword definitions on a September 2026 NCBI metadata snapshot reconstructed in the historical SRAdb schema. Results: The contemporary database contained 41,593,302 experiments, compared with 419,620 in 2013. In library_construction_protocol, the proportion matching all three historical keyword groups declined from 4.06% to 1.42%. The protocol field was NULL in 67.65% of contemporary experiments. Searching design_description alongside the protocol field increased combined three-step keyword detection to 1,197,367 experiments (2.88%), with most additional matches occurring where the protocol field was NULL. Coverage varied across sequencing library strategies, ranging from 0.26% for AMPLICON to 7.69% for RNA-Seq. Independent comparison of 150 sampled experiment records against source XML confirmed agreement in all historical keyword classifications. Conclusions: The original criteria identify a smaller proportion of experiments in the designated protocol field than a decade earlier. Additional preparation-related terminology is detectable in general experiment descriptions, exposing the limitations of searches restricted to one metadata field. Differences among sequencing strategies complicate historical comparisons as preparation methods evolve. The findings support more consistent protocol annotation and the need to distinguish keyword occurrence from the adequacy of experimental documentation.

☆ Escaping cells dilute CRISPR screen responses unequally across cell types
Xuanrui Huang
Single-cell CRISPR screens run in many cell types are used to compare how cell types respond to perturbation, to train models that transfer effects between them and to score such models. These uses assume that cells carrying a guide RNA had their target knocked down. Yet cells grow for days before sequencing: when an essential gene is knocked down, knocked-down cells are depleted or stop dividing while cells that escaped knockdown keep growing, and the measured response, an average over all cells carrying the guide, is diluted. We define the escape fraction of a perturbation as the share of its measured cells whose target was not effectively knocked down, and estimate it from each cell's counts of the targeted gene with a two-group mixture that recovers known fractions in simulated mixtures. In most cell types the escape fraction rises with how essential the gene is, it is higher in a later screen of the same cells, and it reaches about half of the measured cells in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs). It predicts how much each response is diluted: the response size falls to (1 - e)^2 of that of the knocked-down cells. Because the escape fraction differs between cell types, it changes all three uses: hESCs respond like K562 cells unless knockdown depletes them, the coefficient a simple transfer model learns is lowered by the dilution of the cell type it predicts, and a benchmark scored on all cells rewards predictions shrunk towards no change, partly because that ground truth is itself diluted. Where cells stop dividing instead, the response also contains expression differences between cell-cycle stages. Response sizes should be compared on knocked-down cells or corrected for the escape fraction.

Objective: To reduce bias and improve precision in survival association studies using electronic health record (EHR) data when computational phenotypes (CPs) for outcomes and covariates are error-prone and chart review is limited. CP-only estimates became increasingly biased as CP errors increased. In the EHR analysis, MAPS estimates closely agreed with fully validated estimates and improved precision over CRD, particularly at lower validation rates. CP-only analysis suggested increased irAE risk associated with pre-existing autoimmune disease (AID; HR=1.53; 95% CI, 1.12-2.09), whereas the fully validated analysis did not (HR=0.93; 95% CI, 0.67-1.29). Discussion: Precision gains depended on CP quality and validation rates, while small validation samples may affect confidence interval coverage. Conclusion: MAPS provides a flexible and efficient approach to EHR-based survival inference by combining limited chart-reviewed data with error-prone CPs across different validation patterns.

Third, we interpret the dictionary at scale with a reasoning language model, trace how the concepts compose across blocks by gradient-based attribution, and follow the interpreted code to the model's folding output, verifying where the computation aligns with, or departs from, known biochemistry. Together, the sparse dictionaries we train capture the relational geometry the trunk computes beyond the sequence model, and their concept activations forecast the model's own fold quality, turning the black-box folding trunk into a sparse, interpretable, and scientifically verifiable circuit.

Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) has become a standard approach for label-free microscopy of transparent specimens, mapping the optical path length. However, the isotropic phase is blind to the molecular order underlying optical anisotropy. It provides both structural and functional readouts at sufficient frame rates to resolve fast cardiomyocyte contractions. Conventional fluorescent labels bleach over time, perturb physiology, and preclude long-term monitoring. Instead, QPPI enables long-term, label-free interrogation of dynamic cellular processes at quantitative contrast and provides structural readouts similar to those provided by established fluorescent labels, such as frame-by-frame sarcomere length. It also offers previously inaccessible measurements, like quantitative analysis of retardance changes during muscle contraction, which provides a direct optical signature of muscle photoelasticity.

On downstream benchmarks spanning physicochemical properties and target activities, MECo substantially improves consistency by 38-86 percentage points to 90%+ and achieves higher success rates over SMILES-based baselines while preserving structural similarity. Using the full log of one such run over the CrossDocked2020 test-set pockets, we ask whether its keys recur on a pocket the base has never seen and still separate improving from worsening edits. \crchange{Using} the contacts at the site being edited, the action, and the round as \crchange{a} key, the base separates them sharply. Within our analysis, this separation is largely explained by how much the edit changed the molecule's size, the action, and the round, none of which describes the target. That is not because the target is irrelevant: naming it outright separates them several times more sharply. For a pocket absent from the base, transfer must rely on a description rather than its identity. Among the exact-match descriptions we evaluate, the more specific ones rarely recur, whereas the coarser ones provide little separation; the signals that do transfer primarily describe the edit and the molecule it produced rather than the target. Under the representations and lookup scheme studied here, an experience base may be more useful for prioritizing an agent's own proposals for docking than for directly prescribing what to build.

♻ ☆ Probe Before You Edit: Probing-Guided Molecular Optimization for LLM Agents in Structure-Based Drug Design NeurIPS 2026
Zaifei Yang, Weiyu Chen, Yaqing Wang, James Kwok
Structure-based drug design increasingly employs LLM agents to iteratively refine ligands against a target pocket, yet a viable ligand must satisfy two often-conflicting objectives---binding affinity and druggability---which single optimization steps rarely improve together. To quantify this difficulty, we introduce two diagnostic metrics: the first measures how often a single edit improves both objectives, and the second measures how often a gain on one objective comes with a loss on the other. Applying these diagnostics to current LLM-agent pipelines exposes a consistent failure mode: the agent performs molecular editing without knowing how the pocket-ligand complex responds to local modifications, thus rarely achieving joint improvement. Inspired by medicinal chemists, who probe the pocket-ligand complex with controlled analog edits before choosing an optimization direction, we propose \textbf{PROBE}, an optimization framework built around edit--response probing. PROBE first decomposes the ligand into editable sites and builds a pocket-specific \textbf{site map} that flags where joint gains are plausible, where the two objectives are likely in tension, and where liability substructures should be changed; it then performs controlled probe edits whose responses are distilled into an \textbf{EditManual}. Guided by the site map and EditManual, PROBE runs an iterative multi-agent optimization loop. On the CrossDocked2020 benchmark, PROBE achieves state-of-the-art performance and substantially mitigates the failure modes exposed by our diagnostics metrics. Codes are in https://github.com/yzf-code/PROBE/tree/main

We address this problem in two stages. First, in a suitable scaling regime consistent with the Quasi-Steady State Approximation (QSSA), we rigorously establish a stochastic averaging principle yielding a reduced model for the product-substrate dynamics. Guided by the reduced-order dynamics, we next construct a novel Interacting Particle System (IPS) that approximates the product-substrate process at the particle level. This IPS plays a pivotal role in the inference methodology, and we prove several non-asymptotic bounds and limiting results for this system. These results facilitate the construction of an estimator based on a product-form approximate likelihood requiring only a random sample of product formation times. This approach does not need access to the system states, and we rigorously prove consistency of the estimator.

♻ ☆ Curriculum-Augmented GFlowNets For mRNA Sequence Generation

We develop an approach for the de novo synthesis of messenger RNA (mRNA) sequences encoding target proteins. This requires optimizing multiple biological objectives over large combinatorial spaces defined by synonymous codon sequences, a setting where Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods suffer from mode collapse and Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) face sparse rewards over long horizons. To address these challenges, we propose Curriculum-Augmented GFlowNets (CAGFNs), a multi-objective GFlowNet trained with an adaptive length-based curriculum driven by learning progress. In a nutshell, CAGFNs learn from progressively harder tasks corresponding to longer target proteins. We evaluate CAGFNs on CodonDesignEnv, a novel codon-level environment that preserves protein identity via dynamic action masking. Our experiments show that CAGFNs achieve competitive or stronger Pareto-front coverage and diversity while converging up to 4 times faster than non-curriculum GFlowNets, and maintaining 100% sequence uniqueness compared to RL baselines.

Cell-type deconvolution, the task of estimating the proportions of constituent cell types in a heterogeneous biological sample, is a core problem in computational biology. Methods that rely on epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation typically operate on aggregated methylation estimates, discarding the pattern-level information carried by individual DNA reads. Existing read-level approaches that exploit this information are scarce, and all remain restricted to few-class settings; scaling them further is an open problem because, at scale, non-discriminative reads dominate and hard labels conflict with the many-to-many mapping between methylation patterns and cell types, preventing classifier convergence. To overcome this, we propose data-driven soft labels that estimate the conditional cell-type distribution for each read, and integrate this scheme into $Syto$, a new modular framework for read-level classification-based deconvolution. On a whole-body atlas of 39 human cell types, $Syto$ reduces MSE by 3.7$\times$ over the best examined baseline, with gains transferring to an out-of-distribution dataset spanning 16 tissues. $Syto$ lays the foundation for modeling increasingly large cell-type panels, with improved applications in biology and healthcare. The proposed soft-labeling scheme is further translatable to any setting with a many-to-many signal-to-label mapping.

♻ ☆ Quantifying reticulocyte biomechanics in health and disease
Zhaojie Chai, Jianlu Zheng, He Li, Ming Dao, George Em Karniadakis
Red blood cell (RBC) populations are mechanically and morphologically heterogeneous, yet how this heterogeneity governs transport, splenic retention and blood rheology in confinement remains unclear. We combine microchannel experiments with dissipative particle dynamics (DPD) simulations to determine how the morphology, deformability and hydrodynamic interaction of immature RBCs (reticulocytes) shape microconfined flow in acute and chronic mountain sickness. Reticulocyte-rich samples present the three shapes that the maturation literature assigns to successive reticulocyte stages -- multilobular, cup-shaped and near-discocytic -- which we model as R1-R3, each with a membrane shear modulus within the range reported for reticulocytes. A 5-um microchannel resolves these models only weakly, R1 taking at most ~18% longer than control discocytes to cross it, whereas a 1.5-um splenic slit, driven at its own loading, delays R1 by ~30%; both geometries order the models by shear modulus. In cell pairs, a leading cell never lets a follower pass below its own single-cell threshold, ruling out the order-of-magnitude reduction that a wake-"unjamming" picture would suggest; instead the follower queues behind the leader, and a stiffer leader, which clears the slit more slowly, delays it more. The controlling variable is the single-cell critical pressure gradient Delta P_c, which rises monotonically from control discocytes through the reticulocyte subtypes to sickled cells. Set against published rheograms, an analytical estimate attributes chronic-mountain-sickness hyperviscosity mainly to hematocrit-driven crowding rather than single-cell rheology. These results place benign acclimatization, chronic-mountain-sickness hyperviscosity and sickle-cell-trait splenic syndrome on a single mechanical axis defined by Delta P_c.

♻ ☆ Small Average Error, Wide Individual Error: General-Purpose LLMs Estimating Energy Intake from Meal Photos in a Feeding Trial
Xiaomeng Li
Photo-based estimation of food energy could ease dietary assessment, and general-purpose multimodal large language models (LLMs) make such estimates easy to obtain. Most evaluations use one photo taken before eating and compare with energy served, while dietary assessment needs energy eaten. We evaluated eight models from three vendors (Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5; GPT-6 luna, 6.1 sol and 6 astra; Gemini 3.8 Flash and 4 Argon) on 802 meals from ACETADA, a controlled feeding trial with weighed intake, with the before photo only, before and after photos in separate calls (subtraction), or both photos in one request. Three results ran against intuition. Subtraction under-estimated intake for six of eight models, because the models still report hundreds of kilocalories for a nearly empty tray. Scaling the before-only estimate by the average share eaten (0.87) matched much of the gain from the after photo; beyond that constant, the second photo lowered meal-level error by only 2.2 to 4.4 points, mainly in meals with food left. With one photo, two models had a near-zero intake bias only because they under-estimated the served energy and ignored uneaten food. In ablations, adding the after photo improved accuracy under both prompt formats for seven models, while prompt effects varied across models. Over 148 feeding days, five models kept the 90% confidence interval of their mean error within a pre-set 10% margin; one model also met the pre-set 30% limits of agreement, narrowly (-28% to +27%; limits outside 30% cannot be excluded), and the other seven did not. Protein was under-estimated by every model, most in protein-dense meals; repeated calls changed error by at most 1.4 points; a high reasoning effort helped only the smallest model. A low average bias is not evidence of accurate individual intake estimation; such estimates should support, not replace, assessment by a dietitian.

Frontier agents retrieve structural metadata well and compute geometry from coordinates less reliably. We ask how much of a benchmark score reflects that gap and how much reflects the evaluation configuration around the model. We study ProteinGeoBench, a suite of 131 protein-structure tasks, using 4,249 rollouts from four frontier models and 4,486 further trials across 26 models. Three of the four frontier models fall within 0.031 of one another (0.785 to 0.816) with no difference between them resolved, while the fourth scores 0.707 and all three gaps to it exclude zero. Three of the four do better on metadata lookup than on numeric calculation. The fourth is slightly better on numeric. Numeric tasks are 28 of the 131 but half of the twelve tasks that all four models fail. The ranking also depends on the evaluation budget: with one run per task, 23.9% of bootstrap replicates put a different model first. On a selected 15-task slice, removing network access lowers scores more than blocking eight structural-database domains, but the two contrasts were graded in different passes and cannot be cleanly decomposed. Swapping in each model's own command-line agent changes scores by -0.071 to +0.086, a comparison too small to rule out moderate harness effects. Across 26 models, numeric performance rises with non-numeric performance rather than staying flat. The experiments use different task subsets, so they cannot rank model, harness, access and task composition against one another. Evaluations should report results by task family, along with the number of runs, the harness and the access conditions.

The BEST methodology ensures short overall experimental times and highest sensitivity. The method was validated using ubiquitin as a model system, where a precision of approximately 15-20% was achieved at the level of individual cross-peaks. This precision can be further improved by averaging corrected intensities of well-resolved resonances corresponding to the same protein state. The approach was subsequently applied to the quantification of protein concentrations across multiple samples and to the determination of conformational state populations in proteins exhibiting intrinsic or ligand-induced heterogeneity. ♻ ☆ CPTCs Drive Somatic-Visceral Communication via the Wnt Axis in Somatic Mechanotherapy: A Single-Cell Deep Learning Study
Haixiang Huang, Zhenwei Zhang, BingBing Shen, Jianming Yue, Lu Mei, Xudong Zhu, Yonghong Shi, Qianmei Zhu, Yeping Shi, Yifan Luo, Yitong Xing, Meng Dai, Qiusheng Chen

The framework integrates three components: (1) an autoencoder jointly trained with a property predictor to learn a property-organized latent manifold, (2) a denoising autoencoder that projects updates back onto the manifold, and (3) a property-guided Langevin dynamics procedure that performs optimization along the manifold. ☆ What Language Adds, and at What Cost: Four Controlled Probes of Pathology Vision-Language Models
Wenhao Zhang, Zhongliang Zhou, Yi Ping, Zirui Wang, Sheng Li
Vision--language models (VLMs) promise to make computational pathology queryable and able to draft reports, but how much language adds beyond the vision backbone is unclear, because almost every system is evaluated by its developers on test sets of their own choosing. We grade published evidence by how it was produced and test four claims with controlled probes that reuse released checkpoints and public data, varying one input at a time. Report text adds prognostic signal: adding a frozen embedding of the stage-redacted report to a slide embedding raises the pooled C-index by 0.019 for progression-free interval and by 0.016 for overall survival across 1{,}633 TCGA patients, and restoring the stage statement adds nothing. Prompts add no measurable accuracy at inference: with features and pooling fixed, zero-shot classification is statistically indistinguishable from a supervised linear probe for lung and renal cancer subtyping. Slide-level question answering is barely grounded: SlideChat answers 74.82\% of SlideBench-VQA(TCGA) items correctly with the slide and 74.41\% without it, whereas its language backbone alone reaches 43.52\%. Paraphrasing leaves accuracy unchanged but flips 8--23\% of answers. Self-reported gains from agentic navigation and few-shot language priors cannot yet be attributed to language. Language thus adds real but narrow value, and we propose minimum controls that would expose these failure modes in future evaluations.

Living plants, like animals, use electrical signals to carry information about their physiological state across their body, from roots to branches. These signals can be recorded, as they are in animals, from a pair of differential extracellular electrodes inserted into signal-conducting tissue. While machine-learning models have been trained to predict specific plant stress states from these signals, each of these models has been trained for only a single task and none have been designed to transfer across tasks, species, or environments. Here we present Bombadil, a foundation model for plant electrophysiology, pretrained without labels on over 4 million hours of electrical signals recorded from 100 plant species in ten distinct environments, including laboratories, greenhouses, commercial orchards, and natural forests. In this way, Bombadil is able to learn the fundamental features of plant electrical signals across a wide array of species and environments. Then, from those same electrical signals, Bombadil tracks changes in seven physiological indicators of plant stress, even among species and stressors with no labels in training.

☆ Simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic reaction networks
Zekai Li, Mauricio Barahona, Philipp Thomas
Uncovering stochastic reaction networks from data is central to single-cell biology. Simulation-based inference has evolved into a flexible paradigm for this purpose, circumventing the computational intractability of the likelihood. Notably, approximate Bayesian computation performs this inference by carrying out extensive Gillespie simulations, usually at a high computational cost. Here, we propose a simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation (SFABC) framework that avoids both simulation and explicit likelihood solutions of the network dynamics. Instead, SFABC exploits the Chemical Master Equation to formulate a tractable convex optimization with ensuing constraints, which are then used to accept sampled parameters consistent with the observed data. The resulting posterior approximation comes with theoretical guarantees: it can be tightened systematically, and it provably converges to the exact Bayesian posterior distributions. Using synthetic benchmarks, we show that SFABC matches the accuracy of standard simulation-based algorithms at a substantially reduced computational cost. We then showcase the applicability of SFABC to experimental systems biology by analyzing gene transcription bursting kinetics from snapshot, time-resolved, and cell-cycle-resolved single-cell data.
☆ PyGPLA: A Python Package for Generalized Phase Locking Analysis
Amir Khani, Christian Beste, Shervin Safavi
Spike-field couplings measure the links between neuronal spiking and local field potential (LFP) and provide a tool to study how neural populations coordinate activity across spatial and temporal scales. While modern high-density electrophysiology enables the simultaneous recording of numerous LFP channels and neuronal units, this massive scale poses significant statistical and computational challenges for conventional pairwise coupling analyses. The number of channel-unit comparisons grows rapidly, and a coherent population-level structure can be obscured by high-dimensional coupling matrices. Generalized Phase Locking Analysis (GPLA) addresses this challenge by organizing spike-triggered LFP phase information into a complex coupling matrix and extracting dominant low-rank modes. These modes summarize whether a population is coupled to the field, which channels and units contribute to the coupling, and how their relative phases are organized. Here, we present PyGPLA, an open-source Python package implementing GPLA for high-density electrophysiological recordings. Designed for straightforward integration into existing neural data analysis pipelines, PyGPLA supports multivariate spike-LFP coupling analysis, from coupling estimation and interpretation to significance assessment using analytical and surrogate-based tests.

Moreover, the algorithms can leverage any available CPU and GPU resources in parallel for massive computational speedups.

♻ ☆ Propensity Straight-Through Gradients for Discrete Stochastic Systems

We introduce the propensity straight-through (PST) estimator for gradient-based learning through exact simulations of continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs). These models describe discrete stochastic dynamics across physics, chemistry, and biology, but their categorical event choices prevent ordinary differentiation. PST preserves exact forward trajectories and differentiates, in the backward pass, the normalized reaction propensities the simulator already computes. The affine state update makes this rule exact for the one-step conditional-mean sensitivity. We derive the per-step discrepancy for one-step sensitivities composed along nonlinear trajectories in closed form, show that it vanishes for affine downstream dependence, and bound it quadratically in the stoichiometric jump size. Across reversible dimerization, a genetic oscillator, a 50-task repressilator suite, and experimental patch-clamp recordings, PST recovers parameters to within 0.06-1.7% and converges 2.4-3.0-fold faster than the Gumbel-Softmax straight-through estimator at matched computational cost. At deep-learning scale, PST trains all 203,796 parameters of a stochastic reaction network using exact discrete events from initialization. By differentiating an exact conditional mean, PST eliminates reaction-selection temperature tuning and provides a scalable route to learning through exact stochastic dynamics.

On the other hand, despite the initial hypothesis, PINNs fail to match the CRLSM performance and, under the current configuration, do not provide fair parameter estimation. However, we have only studied a limited number of PINN architectures, and it is expected that additional hyperparameter tuning, as well as uncertainty quantification, could significantly improve the performance in future works.

Danqi Liao, Chen Liu, Xingzhi Sun, Dié Tang, Haochen Wang, Scott Youlten, Srikar Krishna Gopinath, Haejeong Lee, Ethan C. Strayer, Antonio J. Giraldez, Smita Krishnaswamy
Generating property-optimized mRNA sequences is central to applications such as vaccine design and protein replacement therapy, but remains challenging due to limited data, complex sequence-function relationships, and the narrow space of biologically viable sequences. Generative methods that drift away from the data manifold can yield sequences that fail to fold, translate poorly, or are otherwise nonfunctional. We present RNAGenScape, a property-guided manifold Langevin dynamics framework for mRNA sequence generation that operates on a learned manifold of real data. By performing iterative local optimization constrained to this manifold, RNAGenScape preserves favorable computational viability proxies, accesses reliable guidance, and discourages excursions into regions poorly supported by the training data. The framework integrates three components: (1) an autoencoder jointly trained with a property predictor to learn a property-organized latent manifold, (2) a denoising autoencoder that projects updates back onto the manifold, and (3) a property-guided Langevin dynamics procedure that performs optimization along the manifold. Across three real-world mRNA datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size, RNAGenScape increases median oracle-predicted property gain by up to 267% and success rate by up to 31%, while maintaining good biological viability proxy measures and achieving competitive inference efficiency compared to existing generative approaches.

♻ ☆ Harmonic Torsional Diffusion for Protein-Ligand Flexible Docking NeurIPS 2026
Maksim Zhdanov, Pavel Strashnov, Vladislav Kurenkov
Molecular docking requires reasoning jointly about ligand pose and protein flexibility. Most diffusion-based docking models predict torsional updates with generic Euclidean heads that ignore the periodic geometry of angular variables. This mismatch is especially limiting in flexible docking, where ligand conformations and pocket side chains co-adapt to form the bound complex. Here, we introduce Harmony, a harmonic torsional diffusion framework for flexible protein-ligand docking. Harmony parameterizes ligand and side-chain torsional score fields as derivatives of learned harmonic potentials on the circle, which are noised mode by mode in the Fourier basis owing to the properties of variance-exploding diffusion on the torus. This construction makes periodicity explicit and gives the model a frequency-aware inductive bias over rotameric motion. On the PDBBind benchmark, Harmony improves ligand pose accuracy and pocket all-atom reconstruction over recent flexible docking methods. On PoseBusters, it improves the physical validity of generated complexes. Case studies on EBNA1 and KRAS G12D illustrate the method's behavior on a polar and a shallow binding site, respectively. Together, these results indicate that aligning the score parameterization with the geometry of the diffusion process is a simple and effective lever for improving flexible docking.
